meta.title: Common Ground
meta.subtitle: Australian federal party policies, side by side — every claim sourced
meta.disclaimer: Independent, non-partisan summary. Positions are paraphrased from the cited public sources and may change; always check the linked source. Not affiliated with any political party.
meta.methodology: Positions were researched from official party platforms, government/minister media releases, legislation and reputable news outlets, then independently verified: every cited source was fetched and checked to confirm it supports the stated position. Positions that could not be verified against a working source are shown as 'No clear position'.

issues.label: Negative gearing and capital gains tax breaks
issues.question: Should tax breaks for property investors — negative gearing and the capital gains tax discount — be wound back?

positions.summary: The May 2026 Budget limits negative gearing to newly built homes and replaces the 50% CGT discount with inflation indexation plus a 30% minimum tax on gains, starting 1 July 2027.
positions.impact_note: Existing investment properties keep today's rules. New investors get smaller deductions; the government expects around 75,000 extra homeowners over a decade.

sources.title: More homes and a fair go for first home buyers
CGT, negative gearing reforms to pass after Labor-Greens deal
Federal measures to tackle Australia's housing challenges explained

positions.summary: Opposition Leader Angus Taylor pledged in his 14 May 2026 budget reply to repeal Labor's negative gearing and capital gains tax changes, branding the budget 'intergenerational fraud' and promising to dismantle Labor's 'housing bureaucracy'.
positions.impact_note: Repeal would restore full negative gearing and the 50% CGT discount for investors, including for properties bought after Labor's rules start.

sources.title: Coalition vows to scrap housing tax reforms and limit migration to supply
Coalition Budget in Reply

positions.summary: Want negative gearing and the 50% CGT discount scrapped for investors with more than one property. Backed Labor's package in June 2026 after winning a ban on self-managed super funds borrowing to buy property.
positions.impact_note: Would strip tax breaks from existing, not just future, investment properties beyond the first — a bigger change for landlords than Labor's plan.

sources.title: Housing | Policy Portfolio
CGT, negative gearing reforms to pass after Labor-Greens deal

positions.summary: Pauline Hanson says the changes will move investment away from housing. One Nation supports negative gearing being available on two properties per person and opposes Labor's capital gains tax changes.
positions.impact_note: Would keep and broaden investor tax breaks, which One Nation argues keeps more rental properties on the market.

issues.label: Low-deposit and shared-equity help for first home buyers
issues.question: Should the federal government help first home buyers into the market with low-deposit loan guarantees and shared-equity schemes?

positions.summary: Since 1 October 2025 all first home buyers can buy with a 5% deposit and no lenders mortgage insurance, with no place or income caps. Help to Buy shared equity launched December 2025.
positions.impact_note: Buyers need a 5% deposit and skip mortgage insurance; under Help to Buy the government contributes up to 30-40% of the price, repaid later.

sources.title: Albanese Government delivers 5% deposits for all first home buyers sooner
More Australians supported into home ownership with the launch of the Help to Buy Scheme
Federal measures to tackle Australia's housing challenges explained

positions.summary: Would keep the 5% deposit guarantee but restrict it to Australian citizens, saying about 50,000 non-citizens have used it. Prefers infrastructure funding and cheaper construction over further buyer subsidies.
positions.impact_note: Citizens keep the deposit guarantee; permanent residents and other non-citizens would lose access to it.

sources.title: Coalition Budget in Reply
Coalition vows to scrap housing tax reforms and limit migration to supply

positions.summary: Opposes the expanded 5% deposit guarantee, citing Treasury modelling that it lifts house prices, but voted Labor's Help to Buy shared-equity scheme into law. Wants a public developer selling homes just above construction cost instead.
positions.impact_note: The Greens oppose the guarantee's expansion; their alternative is government-built homes sold just above cost through a public developer.

sources.title: Labor's 5% deposit scheme will only fuel the housing crisis
Housing | Policy Portfolio

positions.summary: Proposes a government-owned lender operating through Australia Post offering 30-year fixed mortgages at 5% interest with a 5% deposit that could come from superannuation, funded by scrapping the Housing Australia Future Fund.
positions.impact_note: Buyers would get a fixed-rate government loan and could draw on superannuation for the deposit, reducing their retirement savings.

issues.label: Rent caps and renters' rights
issues.question: Should the federal government limit how much rents can rise?

positions.summary: Says tenancy law is for the states. Works through National Cabinet's 'A Better Deal for Renters' — one rent rise a year, reasonable grounds for eviction, minimum standards — and has lifted Rent Assistance instead.
positions.impact_note: No federal cap on rent rises. Renters get one increase a year in most states, plus Commonwealth Rent Assistance that has risen more than 50% since 2022.

sources.title: Better support for renters

positions.summary: Has not proposed federal rent caps or national renter protections. Its 2026 housing platform is infrastructure funding, cutting construction red tape and capping migration to the number of homes built.
positions.impact_note: No announced federal change for renters; the Coalition argues more supply and lower migration will ease rents over time.

sources.title: Coalition Budget in Reply
Coalition vows to scrap housing tax reforms and limit migration to supply

positions.summary: Want a two-year freeze on rent increases, then caps of 2% every two years, plus a National Renters Protection Authority to investigate breaches, fine landlords and advocate for tenants.
positions.impact_note: Rents would be frozen for two years then capped at 2% rises every two years, with a national authority policing breaches.

sources.title: Housing | Policy Portfolio

positions.summary: No published federal policy on rent caps or renters' rights was found. One Nation's housing policy focuses on construction costs, migration levels and foreign ownership of homes.
positions.impact_note: Nothing announced that would directly change renters' legal protections or the rent they pay.

issues.label: Social and public housing
issues.question: Should the federal government fund a large expansion of social and public housing?

positions.summary: Running the $10 billion Housing Australia Future Fund, with Round 3 opening January 2026 to deliver 21,000 more homes toward Labor's 55,000 social and affordable homes commitment, plus $59.4 million for young people at risk of homelessness.
positions.impact_note: More subsidised rentals, crisis housing for women and children escaping violence, and youth housing — though the housing council says supply still falls short of need.

positions.summary: Angus Taylor's May 2026 budget reply would abolish the $10 billion Housing Australia Future Fund and build-to-rent tax breaks, redirecting money to a $5 billion fund for roads, water, power and sewerage.
positions.impact_note: Fewer federally funded social and affordable rentals; money instead goes to infrastructure the Coalition says would unlock up to 400,000 privately built homes.

sources.title: Coalition vows to scrap housing tax reforms and limit migration to supply
Coalition Budget in Reply

positions.summary: Want a federally owned developer to build 610,000 homes over a decade, with 70% rented at no more than 25% of household income, plus $5.2 billion over four years for 50,000 supportive tenancies for people experiencing homelessness.
positions.impact_note: Public rentals capped at a quarter of household income, which the Greens say saves renters up to $16,600 a year, with priority for key workers.

sources.title: Housing | Policy Portfolio

positions.summary: Would scrap the Housing Australia Future Fund and redirect the money into a government-backed lender offering cheap 30-year fixed-rate mortgages through Australia Post branches.
positions.impact_note: Funding now earmarked for social and affordable rentals would instead subsidise home loans for buyers.

issues.label: Cutting building rules to lower home costs
issues.question: Should building and planning rules be cut back in a bid to make new homes cheaper and faster to build?

positions.summary: Backs faster approvals — a 2026 Budget single-touch process combining federal and state sign-offs and a $105.9 million AI tool for environmental assessments — plus a $2 billion Local Infrastructure Fund, rather than cutting building standards.
positions.impact_note: Approvals for new estates and apartments should get quicker, while mandated building standards stay unchanged.

sources.title: 2026 Australian federal budget
Federal measures to tackle Australia's housing challenges explained
More homes and a fair go for first home buyers

positions.summary: Would cut the National Construction Code from over 2,000 pages to about 200, rewrite the EPBC Act and spend $5 billion on enabling infrastructure, claiming the package saves up to $70,000 on a new home.
positions.impact_note: New homes could be cheaper and quicker to approve and build, with far fewer pages of mandated construction rules.

sources.title: Coalition Budget in Reply
Taylor promises 'generational tax reform' and historic immigration cuts in budget reply

positions.summary: Have not backed cutting construction standards. The Greens' supply plan is a public developer building 610,000 homes, paired with investor tax reform; they note Labor intervenes in state planning rules while refusing rent controls.
positions.impact_note: Their platform doesn't propose cutting standards; cheaper homes would come from government-built supply and investor tax changes instead.

sources.title: Housing | Policy Portfolio

positions.summary: Wants a five-year suspension of GST on building materials, points to government charges it says make up 44% of the cost of new homes, and would remove mandatory disability compliance requirements for new homes.
positions.impact_note: Cheaper materials and fewer required features could cut build costs, but new homes would no longer have to meet disability access standards.

issues.label: Foreign buyers of Australian homes
issues.question: Should foreign buyers be banned from buying established Australian homes?

positions.summary: Banned foreign persons, including temporary residents, from buying established homes from 1 April 2025, and in the May 2026 Budget extended the ban to mid-2029, steering foreign investment toward newly built housing instead.
positions.impact_note: Fewer overseas bidders competing at auctions for existing homes, with foreign investment pushed toward newly built dwellings instead.

sources.title: More homes and a fair go for first home buyers
Federal measures to tackle Australia's housing challenges explained
2026 Australian federal budget

positions.summary: No verified current position on the foreign purchase ban. The Coalition's 2026 platform targets non-citizens' access differently — restricting the 5% deposit scheme to citizens and capping net migration at the number of homes built.
positions.impact_note: No announced change to who can buy homes; announced measures affect scheme access for non-citizens and overall migration numbers.

sources.title: Coalition Budget in Reply
Coalition vows to scrap housing tax reforms and limit migration to supply

positions.summary: No current federal Greens policy on foreign buyers was found. The party's published housing platform focuses on rent caps, a public developer and removing investor tax breaks.
positions.impact_note: No announced change to foreign buyer rules; the Greens' proposed changes target domestic investor tax breaks instead.

sources.title: Housing | Policy Portfolio

positions.summary: Would give foreign citizens living overseas and temporary visa holders two years to sell their Australian homes or face repossession, and bar non-citizens, including international students, from future purchases. Permanent residents exempt.
positions.impact_note: Forced sales could add homes to the market; affected temporary residents and students would have to sell or be blocked from buying.

issues.label: Further personal income tax cuts
issues.question: Should personal income taxes be cut further to offset bracket creep?

positions.summary: Labor has legislated cuts to the 16% rate — 15% from July 2026, 14% from July 2027 — and its 2026 budget added a $250 Working Australians Tax Offset from 2027-28 plus a $1,000 instant work-expense deduction.
positions.impact_note: Most workers keep more pay: a $250 yearly offset from the 2027-28 tax year, plus a $1,000 no-receipts deduction worth about $205 on average.

sources.title: Tax reform | Budget 2026–27
Cost of living | Budget 2026–27

positions.summary: Opposition Leader Angus Taylor's May 2026 budget reply promised a "tax back guarantee": indexing the bottom two tax brackets to inflation from 2028-29 and all brackets from 2031-32, costing $22.5 billion.
positions.impact_note: Would stop inflation quietly pushing you into higher tax brackets — about $250 in the first year, over $1,000 a year by year four.

sources.title: Angus Taylor promises to index income tax to inflation in big tax gamble
Grattan on Friday: Taylor's bold budget reply is a mix of sound and dubious policy commitments

positions.summary: The Greens call Labor's $250 offset inadequate (about $4.81 a week, arriving 2028) and want priorities shifted to lifting income support and taxing gas exports and big corporations rather than broader tax cuts.
positions.impact_note: Would shift relief from tax offsets to bigger Jobseeker, Youth Allowance and pension payments, aimed at people on the lowest incomes.

sources.title: Labor's budget backs corporate profits & the 1% over people

positions.summary: One Nation's family tax policy would let couples with dependent children combine and split their income for tax purposes, and would raise the tax-free threshold, cutting tax for single-earner families.
positions.impact_note: Single-income families with children would pay much less tax; workers without children, or couples earning similar amounts, would gain little.

issues.label: Fuel excise relief
issues.question: Should the fuel excise cut be extended beyond August 2026?

positions.summary: Labor cut fuel excise from 52.6 to 20.6 cents a litre in April 2026, halved the discount to 16 cents in July, and let it end on 2 August. Albanese said extension was "not in our planning".
positions.impact_note: Petrol went back up about 16 cents a litre from 3 August — roughly $10 more to fill a 65-litre tank.

sources.title: More fuel relief passes the Parliament
Motorists warned not to expect extended fuel excise cut as Anthony Albanese indicates 'not in our planning'
Australia's fuel discount is ending. What does this mean for petrol prices?

positions.summary: The Coalition backed the temporary excise cuts and says it proposed them first, but when relief ended in August 2026 deputy leader Jane Hume declined to say it should be extended, instead blaming Labor's economic management.
positions.impact_note: Coalition criticises higher pump prices but has made no commitment to bring back the discount, so no immediate change at the bowser.

sources.title: The fuel excise cut has been extended. Here's how much by — and why there's a catch
Fuel excise relief ends as Jane Hume warns Australians will 'feel the pain' at the petrol bowser

positions.summary: No current Greens position on extending fuel excise relief was found. Their 2026 budget demands focused on taxing gas exports, electrification for renters and lifting income support rather than fuel tax cuts.
positions.impact_note: Unclear effect on petrol prices; Greens priorities point to help with electricity bills and income support rather than cheaper fuel.

sources.title: Labor's fuel crisis budget will pick a side: ordinary people or corporate profits
Labor's budget backs corporate profits & the 1% over people

positions.summary: One Nation policy is to halve the fuel excise for three years and reduce freight costs, going considerably further than the temporary relief that ended in August 2026.
positions.impact_note: Would roughly halve fuel excise for three years, cutting pump prices for drivers and lowering freight and delivery costs.

issues.label: Household energy bill relief
issues.question: Should the federal government keep providing direct energy bill relief to households?

positions.summary: Labor let the universal energy bill rebates end on 31 December 2025, with Treasurer Chalmers framing a shift from temporary payments to ongoing relief through tax cuts, Medicare and PBS changes.
positions.impact_note: Households no longer get the federal $150 rebate credited to power bills; no further federal round is planned.

sources.title: Energy bill rebates to be axed in cost of living relief 'shift'

positions.summary: The Coalition attacked Labor for axing the rebates but has not promised to restore them. Its energy plan focuses on keeping coal plants running and backing new refining capacity to lower prices.
positions.impact_note: No guaranteed credit on your bill; relief would depend on wholesale prices falling, which takes years rather than showing up next quarter.

sources.title: Energy bill rebates to be axed in cost of living relief 'shift'
Angus Taylor promises to index income tax to inflation in big tax gamble

positions.summary: The Greens want more household energy cost relief, proposing a 25% tax on gas exports to raise about $17 billion for cost-of-living support and electrification help aimed at renters and apartment dwellers.
positions.impact_note: Renters and apartment residents, who usually cannot install solar, would get help to electrify and cut bills, funded by gas export taxes.

sources.title: Labor's fuel crisis budget will pick a side: ordinary people or corporate profits
Labor's budget backs corporate profits & the 1% over people

positions.summary: One Nation promises to cut electricity bills by 20% through changes to National Electricity Market rules, rather than committing to continued direct government rebates on household bills.
positions.impact_note: Promised 20% lower power bills via energy market rule changes rather than a direct credit on your bill.

issues.label: Supermarket break-up powers
issues.question: Should courts be able to force big supermarkets to sell off parts of their business?

positions.summary: In June 2026 the government formally rejected divestiture powers. It instead banned excessive pricing by Coles and Woolworths from 1 July 2026 and requires ACCC approval for their supermarket acquisitions.
positions.impact_note: Grocery prices policed by a new price-gouging ban with fines up to 10% of turnover, but no forced break-up of the two big chains.

sources.title: Government rejects divestiture in supermarket inquiry response
Price gouging by large supermarkets illegal from 1 July 2026

positions.summary: Under Peter Dutton the Coalition announced court-ordered divestiture powers for supermarkets and hardware in 2024, with competition and public-interest safeguards, and introduced legislation; the policy has not been publicly reaffirmed since the 2025 election.
positions.impact_note: The threat of forced store sales is meant to push grocery prices down, though effects on shelf prices would take years to appear.

sources.title: Coalition government would bring in divestiture power to deal with recalcitrant supermarkets
Coalition announces policy on divestiture powers for supermarkets

positions.summary: The Greens have repeatedly introduced bills giving the ACCC divestiture powers to break up corporations that misuse market power, alongside a bill making price gouging illegal across the economy.
positions.impact_note: Break-up powers would apply across the whole economy, not just supermarkets, aimed at bringing down grocery and other everyday prices.

sources.title: Greens Bills to break up supermarket duopoly and ban price gouging back in Parliament
Labor now isolated in protection of Coles and Woolworths

positions.summary: No clear current One Nation position on supermarket divestiture was found. Its cost-of-living platform focuses on tax, fuel and electricity rather than competition powers over the supermarket chains.
positions.impact_note: Unclear whether One Nation would support forcing supermarket sell-offs, so no predictable effect on grocery competition or prices.

sources.title: One Nation Policies on Issues Affecting Australia

issues.label: Budget repair: spending cuts vs tax rises
issues.question: Should the budget deficit be closed mainly by cutting government spending rather than raising taxes?

positions.summary: Labor's 2026-27 budget ran a $31.5 billion deficit, funding tax cuts by curbing capital gains, negative gearing and trust concessions, plus slowing NDIS growth, rather than broad spending cuts.
positions.impact_note: Medicare, PBS and hospital funding keep growing, paid for by higher taxes on property investors and trusts rather than cuts to programs.

sources.title: Tax reform | Budget 2026–27
2026 Australian federal budget

positions.summary: Angus Taylor's budget reply prioritised budget repair through spending restraint — removing non-citizens' access to 17 welfare payments and the NDIS, and cutting immigration — to fund tax bracket indexation.
positions.impact_note: Lower taxes over time, but tighter welfare and NDIS eligibility for non-citizens and slower growth in government programs.

sources.title: Angus Taylor promises to index income tax to inflation in big tax gamble
Grattan on Friday: Taylor's bold budget reply is a mix of sound and dubious policy commitments

positions.summary: The Greens oppose spending cuts, criticising $37.8 billion of NDIS savings and defence spending, and want revenue raised instead through a tax on gas exports and higher taxes on large corporations.
positions.impact_note: Would protect NDIS supports and lift Jobseeker, Youth Allowance and pensions, paid for by taxing gas exporters and big companies.

sources.title: Labor's budget backs corporate profits & the 1% over people
Labor's fuel crisis budget will pick a side: ordinary people or corporate profits

positions.summary: One Nation proposes a budget savings plan it values at up to $90 billion a year — cutting departments it calls unnecessary, reforming the NDIS, withdrawing from costly international agreements and reducing duplication — with savings directed to infrastructure, debt reduction and taxpayer relief.
positions.impact_note: Large cuts to government departments and NDIS spending; savings would go to infrastructure, lower debt interest and taxpayer relief.

issues.label: Bulk billing incentives for GP visits
issues.question: Should the government keep expanding bulk billing incentives so more GP visits are free?

positions.summary: In government, expanded bulk billing incentives to all patients from November 2025 and added a 12.5% loading for practices that bulk bill everyone. Reports a GP bulk billing rate of 84.1% and targets 90% by 2030.
positions.impact_note: More clinics bulk bill, so a standard GP visit costs nothing on the day; practices that don't join can still charge a gap.

positions.summary: Matched Labor's bulk billing investment dollar-for-dollar at the 2025 election while questioning whether it would really deliver free GP visits. No revised bulk billing policy has been published since the February 2026 leadership change.
positions.impact_note: Signals bulk billing incentives would be kept at similar funding levels, but the current detail and any changes are unconfirmed.

sources.title: Labor and the Coalition have pledged to raise GP bulk billing. Here's what the Medicare boost means for patients
Coalition casts doubt every Australian will 'see a GP for free' under Labor's $8.5b plan

positions.summary: Platform pledges a $21.5 billion boost to bulk billing incentives, including tripling incentives and higher patient rebates, plus 1,000 free public healthcare clinics offering GP, dental, nursing and mental health care.
positions.impact_note: More bulk billed GP visits plus 1,000 free walk-in clinics would mean no gap fee at participating practices.

positions.summary: Calls for higher Medicare rebates so GPs can afford to bulk bill, paid for by cracking down on an estimated $3 billion a year of Medicare fraud, including photo ID on Medicare cards.
positions.impact_note: Higher rebates could mean more bulk billing, but patients would need photo ID on their Medicare card to claim.

issues.label: Medicare Urgent Care Clinics
issues.question: Should Medicare Urgent Care Clinics be permanently funded and expanded?

positions.summary: The 2026-27 Budget commits $1.8 billion to make the 137 Medicare Urgent Care Clinics a permanent part of Medicare, with about $580 million a year ongoing. Visits are free with a Medicare card.
positions.impact_note: Walk-in urgent care stays free and open extended hours, offering an alternative to a long emergency department wait.

sources.title: Federal Budget 2026-27: Key Healthcare Takeaways
Federal Budget 2026-27: A detailed breakdown for GPs
Stronger Medicare and aged care

positions.summary: Said at the 2025 election it would keep every existing urgent care clinic open. No revised urgent care clinic policy has been published since the election loss and February 2026 leadership change.
positions.impact_note: Existing clinics would stay open under the Coalition, though how many new ones would be funded is not currently specified.

sources.title: Shadow health minister Anne Ruston on Labor's health claims
Our Plan

positions.summary: No specific published position on Medicare Urgent Care Clinics. The party's platform backs free walk-in care more broadly, promising 1,000 free public healthcare clinics and boosted bulk billing.
positions.impact_note: Unclear whether existing urgent care clinics would change; the Greens' alternative is a much larger network of free public clinics.

sources.title: Health platform

positions.summary: No published position on Medicare Urgent Care Clinics. Its health material focuses on lifting Medicare rebates, cutting Medicare fraud and getting more doctors and nurses into regional areas.
positions.impact_note: No stated plan for urgent care clinics; its regional focus is on recruiting more doctors and nurses outside cities.

issues.label: PBS prescription medicine prices
issues.question: Should the maximum price of a PBS prescription be capped at $25 or lower?

positions.summary: Legislated a cut in the general PBS co-payment from $31.60 to $25 from 1 January 2026, froze the concession rate at $7.70 until 2030, and funded $5.9 billion of new PBS listings in the 2026-27 Budget.
positions.impact_note: Each general script costs up to $6.60 less than in 2025; concession card holders keep paying $7.70 a script until 2030.

sources.title: PBS medicines to become cheaper by 2026
Major update on $25 PBS cap to make medicine cheaper for millions
Federal Budget 2026-27: Key Healthcare Takeaways

positions.summary: Has not published a current position on the PBS co-payment level. Its published plan and 2026 health statements do not address medicine pricing, and the $25 cap took effect in January 2026.
positions.impact_note: No signal that the $25 cap would change under a Coalition government, but no commitment to keep or lower it either.

sources.title: Our Plan
Latest news

positions.summary: Wants medicine costs cut below Labor's cap: free PBS medicines for concession card holders and a maximum of $7.70 a script for all other Medicare card holders.
positions.impact_note: Would cut a general script from $25 to $7.70 and make concession scripts free, saving regular medicine users hundreds a year.

sources.title: Health platform

positions.summary: No published position on PBS co-payment prices. Its health material concentrates on Medicare rebates, Medicare fraud and regional workforce rather than the price of medicines.
positions.impact_note: No stated policy on what you pay at the pharmacy counter for prescriptions.

issues.label: Dental care into Medicare
issues.question: Should dental care be covered by Medicare for all Australians?

positions.summary: Has not committed to adding general dental to Medicare. Labor's Medicare policy page lists no dental measure, and seniors' groups criticised the 2026-27 Budget for omitting a dental benefits scheme.
positions.impact_note: Adults keep paying full price at the dentist unless they qualify for limited public dental services with long waiting lists.

sources.title: Stronger Medicare and aged care

positions.summary: No published policy to add dental to Medicare. The party's current plan does not cover dental, and its health policy has been under review since the 2025 election loss and the February 2026 leadership change.
positions.impact_note: No proposed change to what you pay at the dentist under a Coalition government.

sources.title: Our Plan
Latest news

positions.summary: Campaigns to bring dental fully into Medicare so everyone can use their Medicare card at the dentist; the platform costs dental in Medicare at $195 billion, funded by taxing big corporations.
positions.impact_note: Essential dental services like check-ups and fillings would be free with a Medicare card, removing a major household out-of-pocket cost.

sources.title: Dental into Medicare
Health platform

positions.summary: No published position on adding dental to Medicare. Its health material focuses on Medicare rebates, Medicare fraud and regional workforce shortages.
positions.impact_note: No stated plan to change dental costs for patients.

issues.label: Medicare-subsidised psychology sessions
issues.question: Should Medicare subsidise 20 psychology sessions a year instead of 10?

positions.summary: Declined to double subsidised Better Access sessions, arguing it would create bottlenecks without more psychologists. Instead funds free walk-in Medicare Mental Health Centres and a free national telehealth check-in launched April 2026.
positions.impact_note: Medicare still covers 10 subsidised therapy sessions a year; free phone-based therapy and walk-in centres are the alternative.

sources.title: Psychologists now want 40 subsidised sessions
Free mental telehealth sessions now up for grabs
Stronger Medicare and aged care

positions.summary: Pledged $500 million at the 2025 election to lift Medicare-subsidised psychology sessions from 10 to 20 a year. The commitment has not been restated during the party's post-election policy review.
positions.impact_note: Would double subsidised therapy sessions to 20 a year, though psychologist shortages could limit how quickly you get an appointment.

sources.title: Psychologists now want 40 subsidised sessions
Our Plan

positions.summary: Platform commits to universal mental health care through Medicare, expanding coverage to more types of mental health professionals, removing session limits altogether and increasing rebates.
positions.impact_note: Unlimited Medicare-funded therapy rather than a capped number of sessions, ending the annual cut-off.

sources.title: Health platform

positions.summary: No published position on Medicare-subsidised psychology sessions. Its health material addresses Medicare rebates, fraud and regional workforce rather than mental health services.
positions.impact_note: No stated plan to change how many therapy sessions Medicare covers each year.

issues.label: Private health insurance rebate for over-65s
issues.question: Should the higher private health insurance rebate for people aged 65 and over be cut?

positions.summary: Budget legislation removes the higher age-based rebate for over-65s from 1 April 2027, cutting rebates by 4 percentage points for ages 65-69 and 8 points for 70-plus, with savings redirected to aged care.
positions.impact_note: Over-65s with private cover face premium rises of roughly $230 to $800 a year from April 2027, depending on age and policy.

sources.title: Health wins and fails for Boomers in the Federal Budget 2026
Removal of private health insurance rebate for older Australians 'a kick in the teeth'

positions.summary: Opposes the cut, calling it a 'health tax on pensioners' and pledging to block it in the Senate. Leader Angus Taylor called it misguided, mean-spirited and 'a disgrace' in August 2026.
positions.impact_note: If the cut were blocked or reversed, over-65s would keep the higher rebate and avoid the scheduled premium increase.

sources.title: House of Representatives, 90 Second Statements

positions.summary: The platform supports phasing out private health insurance rebates and redirecting funds to public health, but the Greens have not settled a position on this bill, backing a Senate inquiry and criticising Labor's funding choice.
positions.impact_note: Their Senate vote helps decide whether over-65s' premiums rise; they argue the money should come from taxing gas exports instead.

sources.title: Health platform
Health insurance saga: Greens welcome inquiry into planned rebate cuts

positions.summary: Opposes the cut, with Pauline Hanson reported as furious about the change. The party has not published a detailed alternative private health insurance policy.
positions.impact_note: Would vote to keep the higher rebate, so over-65s' private health premiums would not rise from April 2027.

sources.title: Senators weigh up private health insurance rebate changes
Health insurance saga: Greens welcome inquiry into planned rebate cuts

issues.label: Net zero and the 2035 emissions target
issues.question: Should Australia keep its legislated net zero by 2050 and its 62-70% 2035 emissions reduction target?

positions.summary: Set the 2035 target at a 62-70% cut on 2005 levels in September 2025 and keeps legislated net zero by 2050, with a $5 billion Net Zero Fund and clean energy funding.
